extracted.intended_audience: students of the Royal Academy; aspiring painters, artists, and connoisseurs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for painters and artists on how to cultivate taste, judgement, and technical mastery through study of nature, continuous imitation of masters, broad learning, and reasoned criticism. Emphasises lifelong study, intellectual industry, and judging works relative to class and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous imitation as method
rubrics_metrics.description: "one continued course of imitation, that is not to cease but with our lives."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infuse your works with what you learn from contemplating others' works; imitate continually throughout life. Anti-pattern: neglecting to look beyond oneself (from indolence, vanity, or business), which leads to stagnation or decline. Example guidance: visit and copy major works regularly (e.g., visit the Vatican frequently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the great masters forever
rubrics_metrics.description: "Study the great works of the great masters for ever. Study as nearly as you can, in the order, in the manner, on the principles, on which they studied."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat masterworks as both models to imitate and rivals to combat; learn their principles, order, and methods rather than merely superficially copying style. Consider masters' excellences as the sources that teach you to recognise defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study nature, but with the masters in company
rubrics_metrics.description: "Study nature attentively, but always with those masters in your company; consider them as models which you are to imitate, and at the same time as rivals which you are to combat."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine direct observation of nature with lessons drawn from masterworks—do not rely on nature alone. Use masters to guide what in nature to accept, adapt, or idealise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry of the mind over mere manual practice
rubrics_metrics.description: "the industry which I principally recommended, is not the industry of the _hands_, but of the _mind_." "Its foundations are laid in solid science."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice must be directed by principle and intellectual study; art is not merely a mechanical trade nor solely a divine gift. Anti-pattern: believing that hand-work alone suffices or that genius alone makes great work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad learning and literacy are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: "A painter stands in need of more knowledge than is to be picked off his pallet... He can never be a great artist who is grossly illiterate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquire knowledge of poetry, philosophy, human nature, and anatomy so your descriptive powers are informed. Reading in leisure and cultivating a poetical spirit enlarge your ideas; avoid becoming a mere craftsman lacking learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation with learned people as important study
rubrics_metrics.description: "conversation of learned and ingenious men, which is the best of all substitutes for those who have not the means or opportunities of deep study."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek out learned company to absorb ideas and form a rational, systematic taste; be curious and docile. This social learning supplements or substitutes for voluminous reading without distracting practical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop taste by reason and fixed principles
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of these studies... the desired and legitimate offspring is a power of distinguishing right from wrong, which power applied to works of art is denominated taste."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat taste as something that can be grounded in reason and general ideas of nature, not as mere caprice. Learn invariable principles so that judgements are not arbitrary; clarify terms to reduce apparent disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the myth that native genius alone suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: "caution you against that false opinion... of the imaginary power of native genius, and its sufficiency in great works."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreliance on innate talent; such belief tends to either vain confidence or sluggish despair. Continuous study and disciplined practice are required for proficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticise masters with independent judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: "study the masters with a suspicion that great men are not always exempt from great faults; to criticise, compare, and rank their works in your own estimation..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form your own standard of perfection informed by masters but willing to recognise their faults; the masters teach you to see both excellences and defects. Do not accept reputation uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imitating contemporary fashions or living masters slavishly
rubrics_metrics.description: "you contracted no narrow habits, no false ideas, nothing that could lead you to the imitation of any living master, who may be the fashionable darling of the day... do not learn to flatter yourselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt fashionable living styles uncritically; favour models that are truly admirable rather than transient popularity. Using one's earlier works as sole models for later work is criticised as self-flattering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for the general idea of nature rather than particularities
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first idea... is that presiding principle... the general idea of nature. The beginning, the middle, and the end of everything that is valuable in taste, is comprised in the knowledge of what is truly nature; for whatever ideas are not conformable to those of nature... must be considered as more or less capricious."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek universal, general truths of nature and human imagination rather than copying particular oddities of individual subjects. Anti-pattern: treating every individual peculiarity as 'nature' (Rembrandt example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not offend the senses; preserve harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: "We must take the same care that the eye be not perplexed and distracted by a confusion of equal parts, or equal lights, as of offending it by an unharmonious mixture of colours..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid compositions that create unpleasant sensory effects (visual confusion, harsh colours, 'splitting the ear' in sound). Even when imitating nature, sacrifice literal accuracy if it produces disagreeable sensations; aim for pleasing harmony and temperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance ornament and purpose; choose the greater reason
rubrics_metrics.description: In large decorative commissions (Rubens example) "all lesser considerations, which tend to obstruct the great end of the work, must yield and give way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the purposes of a work and accept stylistic choices that serve the overall aim—even if they transgress narrow rules. Conversely, be prepared to judge whether the ornament is the artist's proper style or an ill-judged excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the hierarchy of genres and judge within class
rubrics_metrics.description: "weighing the value of the different classes of the art, and of estimating them accordingly... The Roman and Bolognian schools are reasonably preferred to the Venetian, Flemish, or Dutch schools, as they address themselves to our best and noblest faculties."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise different aims and excellences across genres (history painting vs landscape vs colourist painting). A connoisseur should understand what constitutes excellence in each class and assess works against those standards rather than by a single metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer elevation of mind and usefulness over mere ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nor can those works which remind us of the poverty and meanness of our nature, be considered as of equal rank with what excites ideas of grandeur, or raises and dignifies humanity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that unfold useful truths, elevate, or dignify humanity above those that merely delight the senses or display elegant ornament. However, technical excellence in an 'inferior' style can still compensate when done to a very high degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colouring should be true to the eye and harmonious
rubrics_metrics.description: "Colouring is true where it is naturally adapted to the eye, from brightness, from softness, from harmony, from resemblance; because these agree with their object, nature, and therefore are true."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for brightness, softness, harmony, and resemblance in colour so that colouring accords with perception and nature. Truth in colour is judged by natural adaptation and harmony rather than slavish copying of particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the history of the mind and sister arts
rubrics_metrics.description: "This search and study of the history of the mind ought not to be confined to one art only... many things are ascertained which either were but faintly seen... by the practices of a sister art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn from literature, poetry, music, and other arts; analogies across arts reveal principles and inventiveness that inform your own practice. Cross-disciplinary study broadens sources of invention and judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm personal sensations by wider observation
rubrics_metrics.description: "We can never be sure that our own sensations are true and right till they are confirmed by more extensive observation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test your own impressions against the wider public voice and the works that have pleased different ages and countries. Avoid relying solely on solitary taste—seek corroboration to avoid vanity and singularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate imagination and passions by appealing to common feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: "We have no reason to suspect there is a greater difference between our minds than between our forms... there will be... an agreement in the imaginations as in the senses of men."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create works that address general human feelings and passions grounded in shared human nature; use experience and observation of others to know what moves people. The imagination recombines sensory inputs, but must be guided by common human responses.
